title: Lexy
shortDescription: A fully offline, local-first AI personal assistant — notes, reminders, scheduling, and memory, all running on-device.
problem: Managing reminders, schedules, information retrieval, and repetitive digital tasks manually is inefficient — and most AI assistants require sending data to the cloud.
solution: LexAI Butler ("Lexy") is a lightweight, fully offline personal assistant built in Python. It uses a local LLM (GPT4All running Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct) for conversation, SQLite for long-term structured memory, and JSON-based recall for context — no internet connection or external API required.
currentState: Working CLI assistant with notes, reminders (background-threaded, time-triggered), a schedule manager, and short-term conversation memory (last 50 messages) backed by SQLite. Runs fully offline on Windows with CPU fallback. Voice mode is supported but optional/not always enabled.
whatRyanLearned: Local LLM integration without cloud dependency, structuring persistent memory (SQLite + JSON) so the assistant stays context-aware without hallucinating, and background threading for time-based reminders.
roadmap: Long-term direction is turning Lexy into a more autonomous system capable of writing, editing, testing, committing, and pushing code while operating under controlled approval gates — plus expanding voice control, system automation, smart file search, web APIs, and home automation.
note: Do not claim full autonomy unless the implementation actually supports it. Treat as the flagship/featured project.

title: NetCalc
shortDescription: A browser-based networking toolkit — subnet calculator, VLAN planner, and CIDR reference table. Built in a single session, deployed to GitHub Pages.
problem: Network engineers and IT professionals constantly need to calculate subnet parameters, plan VLAN schemes, and look up CIDR prefixes — usually switching between multiple tools or relying on memory.
solution: A pure client-side web app that consolidates three essential networking tools: a full subnet calculator with binary breakdown and subnet divider, a VLAN planner with Cisco IOS config export, and a searchable /0–/32 CIDR reference table. Includes an interactive 10-lesson tutorial for newcomers and a full instruction manual.
currentState: Live and deployed. All three tools are functional: subnet calculator with binary visualisation and subnet division, VLAN planner with auto-subnet allocation and Cisco IOS export, CIDR reference with live search and size filters, and a 10-lesson interactive tutorial with progress tracking.
whatRyanLearned: 32-bit unsigned integer IP math from scratch, binary subnet visualisation, GitHub Actions Pages deployment workflow, and how to ship a complete working tool — with docs — in a single focused session.
roadmap: IPv6 support, ping/traceroute visualiser, export to CSV, and a network diagram generator.

title: BinCalc
shortDescription: A binary calculator and converter that teaches as it calculates — binary arithmetic, hex/octal conversion, bitwise operations, and step-by-step breakdowns, all in the browser.
problem: Binary, hexadecimal, and bitwise operations are core to networking, programming, and IT — but most calculators just give you the answer without explaining how they got there, which doesn't help you actually learn the concepts.
solution: BinCalc is a pure client-side tool with three modes: a Calculator that performs binary arithmetic (+ − × ÷) and immediately shows the result in Binary, Decimal, Hex, and Octal with a full carry/borrow step-by-step breakdown; a Converter where typing in any base updates all four representations instantly with a powers-of-2 explanation; and a Bitwise mode (AND, OR, XOR, NOT) that renders a colour-coded per-bit truth table so you can see exactly what happened at each position.
currentState: Live and deployed. Calculator, Converter, and Bitwise tabs are all fully functional. Features input validation, keyboard support (Enter to calculate), calculation history (last 20 ops), one-click copy, and a fully responsive layout down to mobile.
whatRyanLearned: Binary arithmetic from first principles — implementing carry propagation, signed subtraction, and unsigned 32-bit NOT in JavaScript without any libraries. Also practised writing a complete, polished vanilla JS app with zero dependencies: state management, tab routing, real-time input validation, clipboard API, and accessible markup, all in a single self-contained file set.
roadmap: 8/16/32-bit two's complement mode, dark/light theme toggle, keyboard shortcuts panel, and a binary floating-point (IEEE 754) visualiser.
note: Complements NetCalc — while NetCalc handles IP/subnet math, BinCalc handles the raw binary and bitwise layer beneath it.

title: BinaryGame
shortDescription: A browser-based binary numbers game with four modes — Classic, Reverse, IP Mode, and Blitz — inspired by the Cisco binary game. Race the clock, build streaks, and beat your high score.
problem: Binary and IP addressing are fundamental to networking and IT, but they're hard to internalise by just reading. You need to drill them until the patterns are instant — which is exactly what a game format achieves.
solution: BinaryGame presents four distinct challenge modes: Classic (flip 8 bits to match a decimal target), Reverse (read a binary pattern and type its decimal value), IP Mode (convert each octet of a random IPv4 address to binary one at a time), and Blitz (60 seconds of Classic with no breaks). Each correct answer earns points plus a streak bonus, and remaining time is converted into a time bonus at the end. High scores are saved locally per mode and difficulty. Three difficulty levels (Easy 0–15, Medium 0–127, Hard 0–255) keep it useful whether you're a beginner or drilling for a Cisco exam.
technologies: CSS3 (CSS custom properties, clamp(), dvh units)
currentState: Live and fully playable. All four game modes work end-to-end with timer, score, streak, time bonus, high-score persistence, and a result screen. Responsive down to mobile with touch-friendly bit buttons.
whatRyanLearned: Building game loop logic in vanilla JS — timer management, screen state transitions, streak multipliers, and localStorage persistence — without any framework. Also learned how to make bit-toggle buttons feel responsive and tactile with CSS transitions and active-state scaling.
roadmap: Sound effects on correct/wrong answers, a global leaderboard using a lightweight backend, a hex-to-decimal challenge mode, and a subnet masking drill where you have to identify network vs host bits.
note: Companion to BinCalc — the game drills the speed, the calculator explains the maths.

title: Skybound Sprint
shortDescription: A fast-paced 2D browser platformer inspired by Mario, Celeste, and Rayman. One polished level with enemies, secrets, collectibles, combos, checkpoints, moving platforms, and a full grading system. No assets — everything generated procedurally.
problem: Building a fun browser game entirely without external assets: no sprites, no audio files, no external dependencies beyond the Phaser engine. The challenge was proving that a fully playable, game-feel-complete platformer could be built with only Canvas API art and Web Audio API sound.
solution: Skybound Sprint is a complete Phaser 3 platformer built with 2,000 lines of vanilla JavaScript across 8 modular scene files. All 20+ sprites are drawn procedurally via the HTML5 Canvas API in BootScene. All sounds — jump, land, stomp, damage, collectibles, checkpoint, win, death — and a looping chiptune track are synthesised live via the Web Audio API. The level is a 3,200-unit scrolling world with: a tutorial section, 3 collectible tiers (Stars/Crystals/Relics), 2 enemy types (Walker patrol + Flyer sine-wave), a hidden secret area behind a breakable block, a risky cloud platform route with rare rewards, 2 checkpoints, moving platforms, spike hazards, and a glowing portal goal. The combo system multiplies score for consecutive pickups. Completion awards an S–D rank grade based on time, deaths, and collectibles.
technologies: HTML5 Canvas API (all sprites drawn procedurally)
Web Audio API (all sound and music synthesised)
currentState: Fully playable MVP. Main menu, gameplay, pause, game-over, and win screens all complete. Touch controls work on mobile. Responsive via Phaser Scale.FIT. High scores and best times saved locally. S/A/B/C/D rank grading on completion.
whatRyanLearned: Phaser 3 scene management, arcade physics tuning (gravity, drag, air control, squash-and-stretch), procedural Canvas sprite generation, Web Audio oscillator synthesis for game SFX and music, parallax scrolling with tileSprite and scroll factors, overlap vs collider physics in Phaser, and game loop architecture with event-driven UI communication between scenes.
roadmap: V2 adds double-jump, dash, and wall-jump abilities. V3 adds 3–5 more levels across different biomes (Crystal Caves, Sky Islands, Volcanic Realm). V4 adds local co-op. Leaderboard via Supabase in V5.
note: Built fully from scratch in a single session — zero external game assets, zero build step. Open index.html in any browser to play.

title: Ayana Hill
shortDescription: A polished static storefront for Ayana Hill — a beauty and essentials shop in Kericho, Kenya — built with zero frameworks and deployed live.
problem: A local beauty and essentials retailer needed a professional online presence to showcase products and attract customers beyond walk-in foot traffic.
solution: A fully responsive three-page static site (Home, Products, About & Contact) built in plain HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript. Features a data-driven product catalog, ambient cherry-blossom petal animations, tap-triggered petal bursts, a spinning 'We're Open' badge on desktop, magnifying detail lenses on product cards, and a WhatsApp contact path — all with no frameworks or build tools.
currentState: Live and auto-deployed from GitHub via Vercel. Products page, About & Contact page, and all interactions are fully functional. Continuously iterated with new UI polish.
whatRyanLearned: How to build rich, interactive UI without any framework — using CSS animations, SVG, and vanilla JS for effects like ambient particles, touch bursts, and magnify lenses. Learned fluid responsive design with clamp() and CSS Grid, clean deployment pipelines with Vercel, and how to structure a data-driven catalog that scales without touching markup.

title: SwiftSell v2
shortDescription: A business management platform for inventory, orders, customers, and finances — with real-time sync across devices, Google sign-in, and a fully custom glass + gamer HUD interface.
problem: SwiftSell v1 was a working prototype but had a broken data layer, no real authentication, and a static interface. It needed a proper backend, real data integrity guarantees, and an interface that didn't feel like a generic admin template.
solution: Rebuilt on Supabase (Postgres + Row Level Security) with Google OAuth sign-in, atomic database functions for order creation/cancellation (preventing stock and revenue figures from ever going out of sync), live real-time updates across devices via Supabase Realtime, CSV import/export, and a custom-designed interface with 10 switchable color schemes, a bottom-nav mobile experience modeled on WhatsApp/Instagram/X, and an animated live dashboard.
technologies: Supabase (Postgres, Auth, Row Level Security, Realtime)
currentState: Deployed and functional: inventory, orders, customers, and expense tracking all work end-to-end, with atomic stock/revenue accounting verified directly against the live database. Google sign-in works for approved test accounts while the app awaits Google's OAuth verification review to open sign-in to any user. Live sync, CSV import/export, and an optional Google Sheets export are all working.
whatRyanLearned: Why client-side read-then-write logic is unsafe for financial data, and how to fix it properly with atomic Postgres functions instead of patchwork client checks. Also: Row Level Security design, real-time subscriptions, and OAuth verification requirements (privacy policy, domain ownership, scope justification) that most tutorials skip over.
roadmap: Complete Google's OAuth verification process to remove the test-user restriction; expand the Build Lab-style experimentation into more of the app.
